scenario: The agent audits a YouTube creator's thumbnail series against their uploaded playbook, scores each series, flags any that need attention, and saves thumbnail_audit.csv, series_report.csv, and a style_guide.md.
did: A correct response follows the playbook's own rules literally: it scores each series, flags a series only when all of the playbook's documented flag conditions are met, and writes the three files plus a style guide capturing the creator's consistent habits.
why: Six criteria pin one specific answer when the task's own rules allow more than one defensible reading. C4 and C5 force a FLAG on the Anthony Edwards and Celtics thumbnails, but both have a solid dark block behind the title, and the playbook says to flag only when there is NO dark overlay or solid block behind the text, so the rule-faithful answer is to NOT flag them and just note the inset and red-text problems as issues. C8 and C17 lock the Film Room score at exactly 80, yet the playbook's wording for the palette and face-placement dimensions defensibly supports a 40 or 60 for that episode (the in-game court scene changed both), so pinning 80 rejects a valid grade. C25 and C26 are negative criteria that punish the lower color/face scores, and each one re-scores the same single decision that its positive twin already scores, so that decision is counted twice in opposite directions.
fix: Rewrite C4 and C5 to flag only on the playbook's three documented conditions (and accept a no-flag answer when a solid block sits behind the text); stop pinning the exact 80 in C8 and C17 by accepting the defensible 40/60 readings or grading only the actionable refresh outcome; and drop the negative C25 and C26 so the color and face-placement decisions are each scored once.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The agent chops a run-through video into separate teaser clips per the creator's notes, cutting only the beats marked In Progress, saving them in a clips/ folder with a set naming pattern, and producing a teaser_report.html plus a MEMORY.md note.
did: A correct response cuts one clip per In-Progress beat (skipping drafts and not-started beats), punches in close on the keys beat to match the referenced screen grab while keeping every other clip at the full 1280x380 source frame, and writes the report and memory note.
why: Three criteria have quality problems. C3 bundles two separate claims into a single score: that clip_02 is cropped narrow AND that every other clip stays full-frame at 1280x380, so one score cannot tell which half failed (a model could crop clip_02 right but wrongly crop another clip and still be judged the same). C13 then restates C3's second claim word-for-word, so the check that the other clips stay full-frame is scored twice. C10 is a negative criterion that punishes cutting a draft or not-started beat, which largely repeats the positive C1 requirement to include clips only for In-Progress beats, so that one decision is counted twice in opposite directions.
fix: Split C3 into two separate criteria (one for clip_02 being cropped, one for the other clips staying full-frame) and delete C13 since it duplicates that second check; then either remove the negative C10 or narrow C1 so the do-not-cut-drafts decision is scored only once.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The agent builds a verified itemized cost breakdown of a kitchen renovation for an insurance request, saving renovation_cost_audit.csv (work category, original estimate, actual cost, source) and a renovation_summary.md covering total spend, discrepancies, and anything that looks off.
did: A correct response cross-checks the typed renovation notes against the bank transactions and invoice emails, reports the verified totals and the disputed overcharge, and writes both files so the numbers hold up.
why: The task can be answered from the text and connected data alone, so the images aren't actually needed. Every dollar figure the rubric and tests check traces back to the typed renovation notes, the bank-transaction data, and the invoice emails, so a model can fully complete the breakdown without ever opening an image. The four progress photos contain no cost information, and the handwritten scan just repeats the same numbers already in the typed notes (the rubric even states the scan agrees with the notes). Because nothing in the prompt's actual asks requires looking at a picture, this fails for not depending on the images.
fix: Rework the scenario so at least one required figure can only be obtained by reading an image (for example, put a cost or a discrepancy only in the handwritten scan or a photo and remove it from the typed notes), so the task genuinely needs the visual inputs.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The agent fixes the March tab of a spending tracker with the real bank charges (tips included), then writes a spending_summary.md with the eating-out total, how far over the monthly limit it went, the subscription to cut, and an itemized list, and logs the verdict in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response pulls the actual charges with tips from the connected bank tool, re-buckets them per the user's rules doc, computes the eating-out total and over-limit amount, names the subscription to drop, and records everything in the tracker, summary, and memory file.
why: No issues found — every dollar figure in the rubric matches the connected bank data exactly (eating-out total, the over-cap amount, the subscription figures, and each itemized charge with tips), the negative criterion that guards against altering the Savings or Miso tab correctly penalizes bad behavior rather than a good answer, and all named deliverables and their parts are covered. The receipts are genuinely needed, the unit-tests file is just non-runnable scratch text so the test checks don't apply, and there is no real personal data. No criterion is defective.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: The agent cleans a messy handwritten April toddler skill grid into Toddler_Development_Observation_Report.md, applying crossed-out corrections, counting FC/LC/SC/IC and a total for each of the ten children, ignoring help-needed and absent marks, and naming the strongest classroom skill area overall.
did: A correct response reads each child's row (using the user's turn-by-turn confirmations of the ambiguous handwriting), applies the corrected marks, computes each child's four skill counts and total, and reports the classwide totals with the strongest area identified.
why: No issues found — the per-child counts and totals all match the values the user confirmed turn by turn, the classwide totals and the strongest-area conclusion check out, and every explicit requirement is covered. The criterion checking all ten students at once is the allowed volume check, the criterion about using corrected values mirrors the prompt instruction directly, and the test that only looks for the skill fields nearby is fine because the rubric itself pins the exact per-child values. The PDF must be read, there is no real child data, and nothing the prompt asks for is left unchecked.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: The agent finishes a potter's glaze_reference.md (a 200g test batch for every chart glaze plus a full batch of Floating Blue, with recipe sources and material costs), builds glaze_flashcards.csv and glaze_labels.md, starts a MEMORY.md, and signs the user up for the Saturday wheel-throwing class.
did: A correct response works out each glaze recipe and batch from the chart, wall, and recipe card, sizes the Floating Blue full batch to the limiting material on hand, leaves costs out because the price list was never captured, and produces all four files plus the class signup.
why: There is one small redundancy. C27 is a negative criterion that penalizes any fabricated dollar cost appearing in a deliverable, but two positive criteria (C18 and C19) already score that same no-dollar-costs decision, so the same call is counted more than once. It is kept as a single counted issue because C27 also reaches files the positive pair does not, and the task passes regardless. Everything else is sound: the glaze names, recipes, batch math, cost trap, display-only set, and class waitlist all match the chart pixels and the user's corrections.
fix: Trim the cost-cost overlap by merging C27 with C18 and C19 so the fabricated-dollar-cost decision is scored once (or narrow C27 to only the extra deliverables the positives miss).
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: The agent answers four questions from nine lab photos (what each numbered part on the German reaction tube does, what the titration-screen equation comes out to, what reaction the tube was built to run, and roughly how many vials the analyser carousel holds) and drops it all in answer.md.
did: A correct response inspects the images and answers only what is genuinely legible, saying 'cannot be determined' for the part functions (no legend), the screen equation (too blurry), the reaction (never named), and the exact vial count (carousel only partly visible), per the user's turn-2 demand for honesty.
why: There is one small labeling issue. C6 checks that the agent makes a follow-up image call to re-inspect a specific detail, which is an action it takes during the task, but the criterion is tagged as a 'task completion' (final-deliverable) check when 'tool use' clearly fits better. It is only a label mistake and the check itself is appropriate, since the turn-2 correction asks the agent to ground its answers in a real second look at the images. Nothing else is wrong: the cannot-be-determined criteria line up with the pictures and the user's honesty demand, the two negative criteria each penalize a distinct fabrication, and every question is covered.
fix: Change C6's category from 'task completion' to 'tool use' so the label matches what it actually checks.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.
